q-90794.name: Question 1
q-90794.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2y=0.
$$
q-90794.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+2{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+2=0.
$$

 

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{2}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y=P\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the general solution to the equation d2ydx2+2y=0.

a

dydx=λeλx,d2ydx2=λ2eλx.

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives λ2eλx+2eλx=0eλx(λ2+2)=0. The auxiliary equation is therefore

λ2+2=0.

λ2+2=0λ2=−2λ=±2i

q-79611.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+81y=0.
$$
q-79611.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+81{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+81) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+81=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+81 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-81 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 9\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y=P\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x)+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x).\end{aligned}
$$

q-79611.html:
Question 2
?

Find the general solution to the equation d2ydx2+81y=0.

a
y=Pcos⁡(3x)+Qsin⁡(3x)
b
y=ex(Pcos⁡(3x)+Qsin⁡(3x))
c
y=ex(Pcos⁡(9x)+Qsin⁡(9x))
d
y=Pcos⁡(9x)+Qsin⁡(9x)
e
y=Pcos⁡(18x)+Qsin⁡(18x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let y=eλx. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

dydx=λeλx,d2ydx2=λ2eλx.

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives λ2eλx+81eλx=0eλx(λ2+81)=0. The auxiliary equation is therefore

λ2+81=0.

The auxiliary equation has pure imaginary roots:

λ2+81=0λ2=−81λ=±9i

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

y=Pcos⁡(9x)+Qsin⁡(9x).

q-64693.name: Question 3
q-64693.problem: Consider the equation ${y}^{″}+49y=0,$ where $y=y(x).$ If $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ is a solution, then $\lambda =$
q-64693.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+49{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+49) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+49=0.
$$

Solving the auxiliary equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-49 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 7\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda =\pm 7\text{i}$ are the (purely imaginary) roots of the auxiliary equation.

q-130165.name: Question 4
q-130165.problem: Consider the equation ${y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+6y=0,$ where $y=y(x).$ If $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ is a solution, then $\lambda =$
q-130165.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-4\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+6{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +6) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +6=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +6 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+6 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm \sqrt{2}\,\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm \sqrt{2}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4

Consider the equation y″−4y′+6y=0, where y=y(x). If y=eλx is a solution, then λ=

a
−2±−2i
b
−2±2i
c
2±2i
d
2±i
e
±2i
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Assuming y=eλx and differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λeλx,y″=λ2eλx.

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives λ2eλx−4λeλx+6eλx=0eλx(λ2−4λ+6)=0.

The auxiliary equation is therefore λ2−4λ+6=0.

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

λ2−4λ+6=0(λ2−4λ+4)−4+6=0(λ−2)2+2=0(λ−2)2=−2λ−2=±2iλ=2±2i

Therefore, λ=2±2i are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

q-130171.name: Question 5
q-130171.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y=0.
$$
q-130171.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+2\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+3{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +3=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +3 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1)-1+3 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2}+2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{2}x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{2}x).\end{aligned}
$$

q-130171.html:
Question 5
?

Find the general solution to the equation d2ydx2+2dydx+3y=0.

a
y=e−x(Pcos⁡3x+Qsin⁡3x)
b
y=e−x(Pcos⁡2x+Qsin⁡2x)
c
y=e−2x(Pcos⁡2x+Qsin⁡2x)
d
y=e−2x(Pcos⁡3x+Qsin⁡3x)
e
y=ex(Pcos⁡2x+Qsin⁡2x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let y=eλx. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

dydx=λeλx,d2ydx2=λ2eλx.

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

λ2eλx+2λeλx+3eλx=0eλx(λ2+2λ+3)=0.

The auxiliary equation is therefore

λ2+2λ+3=0.

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

λ2+2λ+3=0(λ2+2λ+1)−1+3=0(λ+1)2+2=0(λ+1)2=−2λ+1=±2iλ=−1±2i

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

y=e−x(Pcos⁡2x+Qsin⁡2x).

q-130169.name: Question 6
q-130169.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+20y=0.
$$
q-130169.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+4\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+20{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4)-4+20 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}+16 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 4\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡4x).\end{aligned}
$$

q-130169.html:
Question 6
?

Find the general solution to the equation d2ydx2+4dydx+20y=0.

a
y=e−4x(Pcos⁡2x+Qsin⁡2x)
b
y=e−2x(Pcos⁡x+Qsin⁡x)
c
y=e−x(Pcos⁡4x+Qsin⁡4x)
d
y=e−4x(Pcos⁡x+Qsin⁡x)
e
y=e−2x(Pcos⁡4x+Qsin⁡4x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let y=eλx. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

dydx=λeλx,d2ydx2=λ2eλx.

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

λ2eλx+4λeλx+20eλx=0eλx(λ2+4λ+20)=0.

The auxiliary equation is therefore

λ2+4λ+20=0.

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

λ2+4λ+20=0(λ2+4λ+4)−4+20=0(λ+2)2+16=0(λ+2)2=−16λ+2=±4iλ=−2±4i

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

y=e−2x(Pcos⁡4x+Qsin⁡4x).

q-90807.name: Question 7
q-90807.problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}-12{y}^{′}+40y=0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?
q-90807.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-12\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+40{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +40) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +40=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +40 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36)-36+40 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -6 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =6\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =6\pm 2\text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

Thus, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{(6+2\text{i})x})={e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{(6+2\text{i})x})={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $3{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ is not a solution.

Question 7
?

Given that y=y(x) satisfies the equation y″−12y′+40y=0, which of the following is not a solution to this equation?

a
−2e6xcos⁡2x+3e6xsin⁡2x
b
3e6xcos⁡2x+sin⁡2x
c
5e6xcos⁡2x
d
3e6xcos⁡2x−2e6xsin⁡2x
e
−3e6xsin⁡2x
Submit
Correct

Assuming y=eλx and differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λeλx,y″=λ2eλx.

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

λ2eλx−12λeλx+40eλx=0eλx(λ2−12λ+40)=0.

The auxiliary equation is therefore λ2−12λ+40=0.

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

λ2−12λ+40=0(λ2−12λ+36)−36+40=0(λ−6)2+4=0(λ−6)2=−4λ−6=±2iλ=6±2i

Hence, λ=6±2i are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

Thus, any linear combination of the functions Re(e(6+2i)x)=e6xcos⁡2x and Im(e(6+2i)x)=e6xsin⁡2x is a solution to the original differential equation.

Among the given options, only 3e6xcos⁡2x+sin⁡2x is not a solution.

q-130330.problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+50y=0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?
q-130330.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+2\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+50{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +50) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +50=0.
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +50 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1)-1+50 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2}+49 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-49 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm 7\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm 7\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-1\pm 7\text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

Thus, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{(-1+7\text{i})x})={e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡7x$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{(-1+7\text{i})x})={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡7x$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $50{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡7x$ is not a solution.

Question 8
?

Given that y=y(x) satisfies the equation y″+2y′+50y=0, which of the following is not a solution to this equation?

a
−2e−xcos⁡7x+2e−xsin⁡7x
b
2e−xcos⁡7x−2e−xsin⁡7x
c
10e−xcos⁡7x
d
50exsin⁡7x
e
4e−xsin⁡7x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Assuming y=eλx and differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λeλx,y″=λ2eλx.

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

λ2eλx+2λeλx+50eλx=0eλx(λ2+2λ+50)=0.

The auxiliary equation is therefore

λ2+2λ+50=0.

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

λ2+2λ+50=0(λ2+2λ+1)−1+50=0(λ+1)2+49=0(λ+1)2=−49λ+1=±7iλ=−1±7i

Hence, λ=−1±7i are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.

Thus, any linear combination of the functions Re(e(−1+7i)x)=e−xcos⁡7x and Im(e(−1+7i)x)=e−xsin⁡7x is a solution to the original differential equation.

Among the given options, only 50exsin⁡7x is not a solution.
